newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open firm, waiting for friendly data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open firm, waiting for friendly data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Wednesday as participants anticipated May economic data that are not due until later this week but are expected to benefit investors banking on signs of a slower economy and continued low inflation.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up as 5/32 to 97-26/32, yielding 6.83 percent in early dealings.
Analysts said short-covering before the May U.S. retail sales report on Thursday and the Producer Price Index (PPI) report on Friday bolstered prices.

"We saw a little bit of bargain-hunting overnight out of Japan and short-covering," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International. "Volume was pretty thin, though. The dollar dropped, as expected, on the Japanese current account data, but it seemed to find a bottom."
Rupert said expectations of friendly data tomorrow and Friday are helping as well. But she added that the market is "still in a fairly directionless range trade at this point."
Firmer European debt markets and "a little bit of a swap bid in London" overnight were supportive factors in early trade, Rupert said.
"There was a little buying overseas and they sort of ignored the weak dollar," said Astrid Adolfson, economist at MCM Moneywatch.
The dollar opened weaker in New York, hovering near its seven-month low against the yen.
Adolfson said she had no doubt that the market would go higher today but said it could turn cautious later in the session in front of the release of influential economic data on Thursday.

The May retail sales data due on Thursday and the May Producer Price Index (PPI) due on Friday are expected to be friendly toward the bond market, which benefits from news of a slower economy and subdued inflation.
Retail sales are expected to be up just modestly after declining in April. The PPI is forecast to be up 0.1 percent.

"We don't expect much today, because there's no economic data scheduled for release and (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan) Greenspan, in his speech in New York last night, talked about the conversion to capitalism in Russia and made no reference to U.S. monetary policy," said Adolfson.
Adolfson said the May U.S. retail sales report on Thursday ought to be especially interesting because of the debate among economists on how much the economy had actually slowed in the second quarter.

"We believe there was pause in economic activity during the second quarter but that it was less significant than some people are suggesting," said Adolfson. "We think if the Fed stays on hold in July, the lower rates and consumer confidence will allow the economy to pick up in the third quarter."
Other factors that could influence trade are hedge fund activity, the dollar and corporate financing, traders said.
In early trade, three-month bill rates were unchanged at 4.90 percent, six-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.21 percent and year bill rates were unchanged at 5.43 percent.

Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-6/32, yielding 6.15 percent. Five-year notes were priced at 100-8/32 to yield 6.44 percent. Ten-year notes were trading at 100-16/32, up 3/32, to yield 6.56 percent.
